name: fsckmd
description:
THE SECOND SLOT-7 CARD BOOTS AND ITS ROOT CHECKS CLEAN.  apple/fgx#408.

Every other fixture runs on the DEFAULT `retronet' card -- standard SmartPort, single-block reads, device subtype $FF -- so a fault that only appears on the extended multi-block path is invisible to the whole suite.  That is not hypothetical: apple/fgx#409 presented as `fsck always finds an issue with /' and was found on a MicroDrive boot, on an image the suite had been calling clean for weeks.  A boot and an `fsck -n' on the other card is the cheapest thing that would have caught it on day one.

THE BOOT LINE IS THE LOAD-BEARING ASSERTION.  `extended SmartPort - multi-block read path (dev subtype $A0)' is what the block driver prints when it has negotiated the OTHER path, and without it this fixture would pass by running on retronet -- a card-selection failure, a missing mdttool or a manifest typo would all look like a green run.  It is the only line on the screen that says which card is underneath.

WHY `-f'.  The root was clean when the kernel mounted it, so its superblock carries MNT_WASCLEAN and setup() answers `file system is clean; not checking' -- fsckroot's note explains the same thing.  Without -f the five phases would not run and the fixture would assert nothing about reading the i-list, which is exactly what went wrong.

WHY `-n'.  A read-only check is all this needs, and it is all securelevel 1 permits once init has gone multiuser (apple/fgx#410).  The point here is whether the READS are right on this card, not whether fsck can repair.

WHAT THE `lacks' ARMS ARE.  The complaints #409 produced on this card and no other: PARTIALLY ALLOCATED INODE, SIZE=0 FILE HAS ALLOCATED BLOCKS, UNREF.  They are what a wrong i-list read looks like to fsck, and they are the reason this fixture exists rather than a generic boot test.

screen_contains: extended SmartPort - multi-block read path (dev subtype $A0)
